title: Worker power: Automation outcomes depend on consultation
desc: Links job quality to organizational choices, surveillance and contestability, without treating consultation as a guaranteed causal safeguard.

kps.k: AI’s workplace effects depend on organisational choices and worker power, not technical capability alone.
kps.d: The cluster shifts attention from how many jobs AI might replace to who controls adoption, how employers redesign work and who receives the gains. The ILO and OECD argue that augmentation can improve jobs or intensify managerial control. Algorithms at Work supports this contingent account with contrasting organisational practices, while the sociological review reports critiques of forecasts that neglect political-economic and cultural context. These arguments reject inevitable outcomes without ruling out displacement.

qs.q: While the technology      can allow the more routine tasks that one does to be automated, potentially leaving time for      more engaging work, it can also be implemented in a way that limits workers agency or acceler-      ates work intensity.
qs.a: Generative AI and Jobs: A Global Analysis of Potential Effects on Job Quantity and Quality (ILO WP 96) and A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure (ILO WP 140) · Academia · 2023

qs.q: Because these studies demonstrate that neither the technologies themselves nor the type of work dictates the ways that employers use algorithmic control systems, what factors do shape this?
qs.a: Algorithms at Work: The New Contested Terrain of Control · Academia · 2020

kps.k: Removing routine tasks can improve safety and engagement while concentrating demanding work.
kps.d: The OECD reports reduced tedious and dangerous work, but also finds that 75% of surveyed AI users in finance and 77% in manufacturing reported faster work. It cautions that pace need not increase stress when workers gain control. A Canadian manufacturing case deliberately retained easy tasks as mental respite; UNISON’s 2025 energy-sector example describes staff handling harder calls without corresponding recognition of longer calls or abuse. UNISON’s cited wellbeing research also reports mixed, context-dependent outcomes rather than uniformly harmful effects.

qs.q: Workers and employers report that AI can reduce tedious and dangerous tasks, leading to greater worker engagement and physical safety.
qs.a: OECD Employment Outlook 2023: Artificial Intelligence and the Labour Market · Regulators & courts · 2023

qs.q: Similarly, experiences regarding autonomy, skill development, and the meaningfulness of work are mixed, highlighting the context-dependent nature of technological impacts.
qs.a: Artificial intelligence (AI) and other new technology in the workplace, including monitoring and surveillance — UNISON bargaining guide (September 2025 edition) · Access to justice · 2025

kps.k: Algorithmic management raises distinct questions about surveillance, accountability and contesting decisions.
kps.d: Algorithms at Work identifies comprehensive, instantaneous and opaque control, including task allocation that encourages constant availability and account cancellation without appeal. Its suggestion that automation narratives can conceal employer choices is an interpretive account, not a universal finding. The OECD and UNISON identify privacy, discrimination and explanation risks even when AI merely advises managers. The OECD nevertheless reports broadly positive assessments among algorithmically managed respondents and some perceived fairness gains. Human involvement therefore matters through the ability to understand and override recommendations, not simply through a manager’s nominal presence.

qs.q: To synthetize these differences, we draw on the four affordances of algorithms introduced earlier (comprehensiveness, instantaneity, interactivity, and opacity), to which we add another key difference: facilitation of the disintermediation of managers.
qs.a: Algorithms at Work: The New Contested Terrain of Control · Academia · 2020

qs.q: Despite being overall positive about the impact of AI on their own performance and working conditions, respondents who are subject to algorithmic management are less positive than respondents who interact with AI in another way (see Figure 4.1).
qs.a: OECD Employment Outlook 2023: Artificial Intelligence and the Labour Market · Regulators & courts · 2023

kps.k: Worker consultation correlates with better outcomes, but the evidence does not establish a causal guarantee.
kps.d: The ILO links stronger European consultation institutions with greater openness to adoption. The OECD’s separate 2022 survey of manufacturing and finance workers across seven countries finds that workers in consulting firms were nine percentage points more likely to report improved health and safety. Its European establishment analysis also associates representation with better conditions, but flags descriptive designs and possible reverse causality. Algorithms at Work treats applying participation and training approaches specifically to algorithmic systems as a research agenda. Together, these sources support investigating and resourcing worker voice rather than claiming consultation invariably delivers benefits.

qs.q: Studies on Europe have shown that it is the countries with stronger and more coop-      erative forms of workplace consultation, essentially the Nordic countries, followed by Germany,      where workers are more open to technological adoption at the workplace.
qs.a: Generative AI and Jobs: A Global Analysis of Potential Effects on Job Quantity and Quality (ILO WP 96) and A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure (ILO WP 140) · Academia · 2023

qs.q: For example, workers in companies that consulted workers or worker representatives are 9 percentage points more likely to say that AI had improved their health and safety, compared to workers in companies that did not consult workers or workers representatives.
qs.a: OECD Employment Outlook 2023: Artificial Intelligence and the Labour Market · Regulators & courts · 2023

kps.k: The policy debate concerns the strength and design of safeguards, with different employer and union priorities.
kps.d: The ILO advocates enforceable workplace rules and equal-voice governance by workers, employers and governments. The OECD treats regulation as a minimum foundation that bargaining can develop, while recognising existing legal protections and uncertainty about necessary adaptations. Its non-representative 2022 questionnaire records unions prioritising ethical threats and employers emphasising skills, with variation within both groups. UNISON advocates stronger consultation, explanation, human-review and disconnect rights through the proposed TUC employment-AI Bill. Its emphasis on informed consent faces the OECD’s qualification that employment power imbalances can make refusal difficult; these are differences in emphasis and institutional design, not a simple pro- versus anti-AI divide.

qs.q: The design      and application of such regulations is best crafted through tripartite systems, in which workers’,      employers’ and governments representatives engage with equal voice.
qs.a: Generative AI and Jobs: A Global Analysis of Potential Effects on Job Quantity and Quality (ILO WP 96) and A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure (ILO WP 140) · Academia · 2023

qs.q: In this respect, regulations and social dialogue can complement each other, for example when AI-related regulations set minimum standards and specify terms that require further dialogue and bargaining.
qs.a: OECD Employment Outlook 2023: Artificial Intelligence and the Labour Market · Regulators & courts · 2023

kps.k: Practical governance requires continuing oversight, representative capacity and negotiated transition support.
kps.d: UNISON proposes participation from procurement through deployment and review, accessible system records, pilots, repeated impact assessments, independent expertise and human review. It seeks funded retraining, redeployment, appropriate pay for more demanding roles and shared productivity gains. The OECD documents existing precedents, including Spain’s 2021 banking agreement on solely algorithmic decisions and the Teamsters–UPS technological-change committee. However, declining representation and limited technical resources constrain bargaining. Few AI-specific agreements need not indicate inaction where existing protections already apply. UNISON’s model terms remain proposals requiring workplace adaptation, not evidence of universal practice.

qs.q: Ideally the union is involved in   discussions early in considerations when new technology is to be introduced - in   the design, procurement, trial, implementation, review and maintenance.
qs.a: Artificial intelligence (AI) and other new technology in the workplace, including monitoring and surveillance — UNISON bargaining guide (September 2025 edition) · Access to justice · 2025

qs.q: In Spain, social partners in the banking sector signed an agreement in 2021 guaranteeing  workers the right to not be subject to decisions taken solely by algorithmic systems, nor discriminated  against based on algorithmic decisions.
qs.a: OECD Employment Outlook 2023: Artificial Intelligence and the Labour Market · Regulators & courts · 2023

kps.k: Creating AI-related work does not ensure secure employment or adequate protections.
kps.d: The ILO predicts that lower LLM entry barriers could expand demand for domain-specific datasets curated by microtask workers; it does not report measured employment growth. It distinguishes direct hiring from crowdsourced, task-paid civil contracts that lack employment-linked protections. Algorithms at Work likewise describes flexibility coexisting with low pay, isolation and exhaustion, while documenting variation across platforms and workers. The practical implication is to address contractual protection and representation alongside job creation. The ILO reports a planned two-year platform-work standard-setting process beginning in 2025, not a completed standard.

qs.q: This      dramatic decrease in the cost and ease of entry to the LLM market points to an increase in de-      mand for domain-specific labelled datasets curated by microtask workers.
qs.a: Generative AI and Jobs: A Global Analysis of Potential Effects on Job Quantity and Quality (ILO WP 96) and A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure (ILO WP 140) · Academia · 2023

qs.q: Finally, although platforms may afford workers high levels of flexibility, autonomy, and task variety, these benefits are often coupled with low pay, social isolation, irregular work hours, and exhaustion (Wood et al., 2019).
qs.a: Algorithms at Work: The New Contested Terrain of Control · Academia · 2020

kps.k: The evidence supports a contingent account of workplace change, not a settled generative-AI employment forecast.
kps.d: The OECD’s 2023 baseline finds clearer effects on job quality than employment levels, largely using evidence predating recent generative AI; its workplace surveys cover only finance and manufacturing and cannot eliminate worker-selection effects. Exposure measures and workers’ fears do not establish displacement. The sociological review contrasts large replacement forecasts with Petterson’s tacit-knowledge argument for knowledge-worker resilience, but supplies no methods or quantitative results for that contention. UNISON expects more role transformation than elimination while reporting a local headcount-reduction case. These different evidence types cannot establish either universal professional immunity or inevitable mass job loss, including in legal work.

qs.q: So far, job quality has been impacted more than job quantity  Based on the current literature (which mostly predates the latest wave of generative AI), there is little evidence of significant negative employment effects due to AI so far.
qs.a: OECD Employment Outlook 2023: Artificial Intelligence and the Labour Market · Regulators & courts · 2023

qs.q: For instance, Petterson (2019) analyses the use of AI in “knowledge work”, work that requires sophisticated problem‐solving capabilities, and contends that AI will not threaten human “knowledge workers”, for it lacks the human expert's ability to deploy tacit knowledge to assess and resolve problems.
qs.a: Sociological perspectives on artificial intelligence: A typological reading · Academia · 2021

vlens.an: The selected academia and research sources collectively accept the proposition’s contingent account: workplace outcomes are shaped by organisational design, worker power and social context rather than technical capability alone. They materially develop it in three ways. First, the labour-process analysis identifies distinctive mechanisms of algorithmic control—especially opacity, intensive monitoring and constrained contestability—and shows that contrasting managerial practices can produce different worker experiences. Second, the sociological review supplies the broader critique of technologically deterministic employment forecasts, although it contributes less directly to the proposition’s claims about consultation and governance. Third, the ILO analysis turns worker voice into a more concrete institutional programme by coupling workplace participation with enforceable protections, post-deployment oversight and equal-voice tripartite governance. Material internal variation concerns evidential strength and emphasis: some organisational examples document observed worker outcomes, whereas consultation benefits are partly correlational or framed as research questions; the sociological source stresses context and individual adaptability, while the labour-process and ILO sources place greater weight on structural power, surveillance, collective representation and regulation. These curated sources therefore build on the proposition without establishing that consultation invariably causes better outcomes.

qs.q: Because these studies demonstrate that neither the technologies themselves nor the type of work dictates the ways that employers use algorithmic control systems, what factors do shape this?
qs.a: Algorithms at Work: The New Contested Terrain of Control · Academia · 2020

vlens.an: The selected civil-society source, UNISON’s bargaining guide, accepts the proposition that AI’s effects on job quality are contingent on organisational choices and worker power rather than predetermined by the technology. It materially extends the proposition by specifying how worker influence should operate across the technology lifecycle: early consultation, disclosure and system mapping, pilots, recurring impact assessments, access to independent expertise, human review, retraining, redeployment and sharing productivity gains. Its reasoning centres on workers’ ability to identify, understand and contest systems that may otherwise intensify work, expand surveillance, reproduce discrimination or obscure responsibility. There is important variation within this broadly supportive account: UNISON recognises that automation can remove tedious tasks, improve services and transform more jobs than it eliminates, while also reporting displacement and intensified work in particular cases. It therefore treats beneficial outcomes as implementation-dependent. Its governance measures are principally bargaining and legislative proposals, not evidence that consultation itself guarantees better outcomes, which is consistent with the cluster’s caution about causality. This assessment concerns the supplied UNISON source and should not be generalised to civil-society organisations as a whole.

qs.q: Whether this positive vision is realised depends greatly on how the technology is to be implemented.

vlens.an: The OECD source supports the proposition that workplace outcomes depend on organisational implementation and worker power rather than AI capability alone. It reports an association between consultation and improved health-and-safety outcomes, while explicitly declining to treat that association as causal. Its broader reasoning reinforces the cluster’s emphasis on meaningful human oversight, contestability, collective bargaining and regulation, particularly where algorithmic management may intensify work, reduce autonomy or impede redress. Material variation lies within the OECD’s evidence: AI can remove tedious or dangerous tasks and improve perceived fairness, yet it can also accelerate work and expand surveillance; consultation appears beneficial, but cross-sectional design, possible reverse causality and limited sector coverage prevent any claim that it guarantees better outcomes. This assessment concerns the OECD source in the curated corpus and should not be generalized to all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: For example, workers in companies that consulted workers or worker representatives are 9 percentage points more likely to say that AI had improved their health and safety, compared to workers in companies that did not consult workers or workers representatives.
qs.a: OECD Employment Outlook 2023: Artificial Intelligence and the Labour Market · Regulators & courts · 2023

elens.an: The curated 2015–2022 sources collectively accept the proposition’s core contingent account: automation outcomes are shaped by organisational design, political-economic and socio-cultural context, and worker agency rather than by technical capability alone. They build on it chiefly through Algorithms at Work, which develops a labour-process account of algorithmic control, identifies opacity and constrained contestability as distinctive worker risks, contrasts managerial arrangements producing different outcomes, and advances worker voice, training and collective governance as concrete research priorities. Material internal variation remains. Algorithms at Work directly examines organisational practices, surveillance, precarity and resistance, while the sociological review offers broader support by criticising technologically deterministic displacement forecasts and highlighting context, tacit knowledge and adaptability, but does not substantially develop the proposition’s consultation or governance claims. Moreover, participation and training are presented as promising approaches or research questions, not as proven causal safeguards; worker experiences also vary, with some reporting autonomy and flexibility alongside evidence of low pay, exhaustion and difficulty resisting control.

qs.q: Because these studies demonstrate that neither the technologies themselves nor the type of work dictates the ways that employers use algorithmic control systems, what factors do shape this?
qs.a: Algorithms at Work: The New Contested Terrain of Control · Academia · 2020

elens.an: The 2023–2024 sources support the cluster’s principal proposition that workplace outcomes depend materially on organisational implementation and worker power rather than AI capability alone. Both the ILO and OECD describe a contingent pathway: automation may remove routine or dangerous tasks and improve engagement, but it may also intensify work, reduce autonomy and expand surveillance or unaccountable managerial control. They therefore treat meaningful worker participation, human oversight and the ability to contest decisions as important safeguards, while pairing consultation with regulation, collective bargaining and institutional capacity. Material variation lies mainly in evidentiary confidence and policy emphasis. The ILO states the dependence on worker voice more directly and advances enforceable, tripartite governance. The OECD is more empirically cautious: it reports associations between consultation and better outcomes but stresses that its cross-sectional, largely pre-generative-AI evidence does not establish causality and may not generalise across sectors or newer systems. Thus, these curated sources converge on the proposition without claiming that consultation guarantees beneficial outcomes or settles generative AI’s employment effects.

qs.q: As a result, whether the effect of technology on working      conditions is positive or negative depends in large part on the voice that workers have in the      design, implementation and use of technology.
qs.a: Generative AI and Jobs: A Global Analysis of Potential Effects on Job Quantity and Quality (ILO WP 96) and A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure (ILO WP 140) · Academia · 2023

qs.q: Although the analysis controls for an extensive set of variables, it remains descriptive and mostly serves as a motivation to investigate further any causal relation between workers’ voice and the AI transition.

elens.an: The September 2025 UNISON guide accepts the cluster’s principal proposition that workplace outcomes are contingent on organisational choices and worker power rather than determined by AI’s technical capabilities. It materially extends that proposition by translating worker consultation into a concrete governance programme: early union involvement across design, procurement, trials, implementation, maintenance and review; system disclosure; repeated impact assessments; access to independent expertise; human review; negotiated retraining and redeployment; and sharing productivity gains. Its reasoning is that these mechanisms can reduce information asymmetry, make surveillance and algorithmic decisions contestable, and protect job quality during restructuring. Material variation within the guide prevents a deterministic reading: it recognises possible efficiency, safety and task-quality benefits, expects role transformation more often than whole-job elimination, and reports context-dependent wellbeing effects, while also documenting work intensification, surveillance, discrimination risks and a local headcount reduction. UNISON therefore advocates consultation and enforceable safeguards as practical means of shaping adoption, but largely presents them as proposed protections rather than evidence that consultation necessarily causes beneficial outcomes.
